name: 3D Printing

claims.claim_text: The RepRap project was deliberately designed so that almost every part of the machine could be produced by the machine itself, making it self-replicating apart from the drive electronics.
claims.quote_verbatim: they deliberately designed that using almost all parts that can actually be made by the machine itself
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Agilent, Analog, Cold Fusion - Funding Fusion Is Not Futile

claims.claim_text: The RepRap project solved most of the hard technical problems of desktop extrusion printing before the commercial desktop industry began around 2009, and the companies that followed took that technology, improved it incrementally and built businesses on it.
claims.quote_verbatim: the RepRap guys had gone and figured out most of the hard technical problems
claims.speaker: Ariel Briner
claims.episode_title: An interview with Ariel Briner of Cartesian Co

claims.claim_text: Fused-deposition print speed is bounded by the thermal properties of the plastic: each layer must harden just enough for the next to be laid on cleanly without smushing, which imposes a physical limit that cannot be engineered away.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's really no good way to speed it up because it's based on the thermal properties of the plastic
claims.speaker: Chris Anderson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Anderson - Deambulatory Daedal Drones

claims.claim_text: Laser curing of a liquid resin is not subject to the same thermal constraint as extrusion, so it has physical limits that are far less restrictive on speed.
claims.quote_verbatim: You sort of need the plastic to harden just enough in each layer so the next layer comes on cleanly without smushing.
claims.speaker: Chris Anderson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Anderson - Deambulatory Daedal Drones

claims.claim_text: Powder-based processes work by depositing a liquid binder onto a powder bed in the manner of an inkjet, producing a sludge that is subsequently baked.
claims.quote_verbatim: you kind of like put liquid on top of the powder and it creates this like sludge and then you kind of bake it
claims.speaker: Chris Anderson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Anderson - Deambulatory Daedal Drones

claims.claim_text: Additive fabrication is a raster process whose time scales as the area to be covered multiplied by the number of passes over it, against the speed of the head, and head speed is itself bounded by the accuracy that must be maintained; that arithmetic is why it does not suit production volumes.
claims.quote_verbatim: the fastest you're going to go is going to be the total area you have to cover times how many times
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: CAD courses and cross platform creation - Printing Propaedeutic Patterns

claims.claim_text: The speed ceiling of a raster deposition process comes down to how fast the head can be physically moved while still holding the required process accuracy.
claims.quote_verbatim: it comes down to how fast you can physically move the head across and still maintain your, uh, your accuracy
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: CAD courses and cross platform creation - Printing Propaedeutic Patterns

claims.claim_text: The term covers no coherent list of manufacturing technologies: desktop extrusion machines sit alongside laser metal powder bed fusion, the process behind aerospace and medical components, and directed energy deposition, which builds large metal structures with robotic arms.
claims.quote_verbatim: the term 3D printing doesn't refer to any coherent list of manufacturing technologies

claims.claim_text: Laser metal powder bed fusion is the standard process for aerospace and medical metal components, and directed energy deposition is what allows very large metal structures to be built up.
claims.quote_verbatim: laser metal powder bed fusion

claims.claim_text: Printable polymers are low-temperature and low tensile strength materials, which is the standing constraint on where printed parts can substitute for metal ones.
claims.quote_verbatim: all printable material are low temp and low tensile strength
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: FPGA, Xess, 32 Bit - Quirky Qualitative Questions

claims.claim_text: Printed plastic parts are weak enough that a mechanism built from them can fail under ordinary motor loads: printed carriages snapped in half when the motor was first energised, and the work moved to aluminium extrusion instead.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'll turn the motor on and I'll have snapped it right in half
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Noah Feehan - Biloquistic Blinking Blush

claims.claim_text: A resin machine left running overnight produces functional parts at roughly fifty micron resolution with material properties adequate for function, though not equivalent to injection-moulded ABS.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's good enough where you can basically make functional parts
claims.speaker: Ben Krasnow
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ben Krasnow, 8 years on

claims.claim_text: The dominant electronics application is custom enclosures and shells, which are difficult to produce even with a good CNC milling machine.
claims.quote_verbatim: 3D printing is especially good for shells and project enclosures
claims.speaker: Ben Krasnow
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ben Krasnow - Sprauncy Saccadic Spintherism

claims.claim_text: The competing practice is to design the product around an off-the-shelf enclosure, because such enclosures cost a dollar or two, are available in every country and require no design effort of their own.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm a huge fan of using off-the-shelf enclosures and designing your product around that
claims.speaker: Ben Krasnow
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ben Krasnow - Sprauncy Saccadic Spintherism

claims.claim_text: In consulting work the recommended default is to take a suitable off-the-shelf case and design the board to fit it, because case design consumes hours that are difficult to bill and invites open-ended tweaking.
claims.quote_verbatim: just get a damn case which looks suitable off the shelf and then just design your board around that
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Designing an enclosure in house tends to produce a worse part than an enclosure vendor's, because the vendor's mechanical engineers design for draft angles and manufacturability at high volume in a way an electronics engineer does not.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm just not as good as, like, some engineer at BudBoxes that is designing this thing with draft angles
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The characteristic failure of designing an enclosure only against a printer is that the printed prototype cannot be manufactured by the production process it is later handed to.
claims.quote_verbatim: when you're finally going to production, the production house says, we can't build this
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A prototype optimised for hand assembly and printing is effectively a different design from the manufacturable version, so schedule and iteration have to be budgeted for design for manufacture and for trial runs with the real suppliers.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't expect that the version that you prototyped is going to be the same version that you go to production with
claims.speaker: Chrissy Meyer

claims.claim_text: Mechanical design for manufacture cannot be done in isolation from the supplier: it is a sustained exchange about what the supplier can and cannot do and what its mould flow analysis shows, and on a complex product that exchange can run for months before a part is released.
claims.quote_verbatim: DFM is not something that you can do in a vacuum
claims.speaker: Chrissy Meyer

claims.claim_text: A part that is painful to print — full of undercuts and thin walls — may be trivial by another process such as heat-folding sheet plastic over a nichrome wire, so a designer needs a mental library of manufacturing methods kept in sync with what the chosen supplier actually owns.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're going to have a terrible time with all the undercuts
claims.speaker: Chrissy Meyer

claims.claim_text: Knowing the vocabulary of standard mechanical parts and methods is what prevents wasted printing: not knowing the name of the right component leads to spending weeks printing a jig for a problem that had a standard solution.
claims.quote_verbatim: you spend four weeks doing the jig and then you find out there is a way easier way to do it
claims.episode_title: Grad School Time Capsule with Joshua and Zach

claims.claim_text: Printing is close to unconstrained in geometry apart from overhangs and the support material they require, machining carries real geometric limitations, and any moulded part needs draft or taper so that it will release from the mould, which CAD draft analysis tools check for.
claims.quote_verbatim: 3d printing tends to be limitless with the exception of things like overhang
claims.speaker: John Saunders

claims.claim_text: Moulded parts require draft or taper so the part can come out of the mould, a constraint printing does not impose and which therefore has to be added deliberately when a printed design is moved to moulding.
claims.quote_verbatim: you need to have some draft or taper so that the part will actually come out of the mold
claims.speaker: John Saunders

claims.claim_text: Between printing and injection moulding sit low-pressure moulding processes that avoid the multi-hundred-ton clamping pressure of injection moulding and serve both testing and small-run production.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's a ton of ways to mold things that are not under the multi hundred ton pressure of injection molding
claims.speaker: John Saunders

claims.claim_text: An alternative prototype route for small mechanical parts is to machine a positive master, cast a silicone negative from it and pour urethane into that, which was used to prototype miniature planetary gear sets.
claims.quote_verbatim: he machines out this positive mold. And then he pours a negative mold with silicone. And then he pours urethane into that
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Because a new mould is expensive, injection moulding penalises design variation, whereas printing makes cheap one-offs; that asymmetry is what makes parametric modelling valuable, since engineer time spent generating variants is the cheap part.
claims.quote_verbatim: with 3D printing, you can do very cheap one-offs
claims.speaker: Claire Wolf

claims.claim_text: Mould making has itself become cheap enough to compete: a five-axis machine can cut a soft-metal or steel mould for hundreds of dollars, and cast-off moulds can be bought second hand and modified by welding on a new gate.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can churn out a mold and like a steel mold for hundreds of bucks
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Printing production enclosures does not scale: printing the cases for a funded hardware product meant running several machines continuously to produce hundreds and eventually close to a thousand parts, covering the main case and every accessory enclosure, and the second version of the product moved to injection moulding.
claims.quote_verbatim: It was hundreds. Because it wasn't like in the hundreds, if not just under a thousand.
claims.speaker: Marcus Schappi
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Marcus Schappi - Kit Ketch Kenophobia

claims.claim_text: Printed cases are a reasonable production choice only at volumes of roughly ten units or fewer.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's a good idea if no one buys it. Or if one person buys it. Or if 10 people buy it.
claims.speaker: Marcus Schappi
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Marcus Schappi - Kit Ketch Kenophobia

claims.claim_text: The same programme moved to injection moulding for its second version, which brought its own problems but was decisively better than printing at that volume.
claims.quote_verbatim: for the second version of the Ninja Block, we did injection molding
claims.speaker: Marcus Schappi
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Marcus Schappi - Kit Ketch Kenophobia

claims.claim_text: Frame rigidity governs dimensional accuracy: the contemporary advice was to avoid the wood-framed machine, because wood flexes, and to buy a rigid-framed printer where accuracy mattered.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's made out of wood and, you know, wood flexes. And if you want accuracy, you should go and buy the UP printer
claims.speaker: Marcus Schappi
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Marcus Schappi - Kit Ketch Kenophobia

claims.claim_text: Printers emit fumes strong enough to be a siting constraint; one production printing effort was run outdoors on a balcony because the smell was intolerable indoors.
claims.quote_verbatim: we started off 3D printing, you know, all the enclosures on our balcony
claims.speaker: Marcus Schappi
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Marcus Schappi - Kit Ketch Kenophobia

claims.claim_text: Printed production parts also disappoint on finish quality, which together with the machine-tending burden is why the practitioners who have done it describe it as not to be repeated.
claims.quote_verbatim: he said that was the biggest never, never again
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Stereolithography consumables are the limiting cost at small production volumes: a kilogram bottle of resin at around a hundred and fifty dollars yields roughly twenty prints, and a detailed enclosure takes three or four hours of machine time per part.
claims.quote_verbatim: you get like, I don't know, 20 prints out of it, but it's 150 bucks
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A detailed printed case takes on the order of three to four hours per part, which sets the throughput ceiling when printing is used for anything beyond single units.
claims.quote_verbatim: to print a nice detailed case is like three, four hours
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Filament costs around twenty dollars a kilogram on a spool while commercial bureau printing was priced around five dollars per cubic inch, and a good commercial machine ran to about fifteen thousand dollars fully equipped in the early 2010s.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's like $5 per cubic inch
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Bulk feedstock is cheap relative to bureau pricing: about twenty dollars for a kilogram of ABS on a spool.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's only about $20 for a kilo of ABS plastic on a spool
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Stereolithography machines fell from a couple of hundred thousand dollars to around ten thousand during the 2010s, and a Chinese desktop machine at about two thousand four hundred dollars in 2012 was the entry point that made ownership plausible for an individual designer.
claims.quote_verbatim: when they were a couple hundred thousand dollars
claims.speaker: Julia Truchsess

claims.claim_text: The practical change the technology brought to mechanical prototyping was replacing hot-gluing sheet plastic and hobby-shop parts with drawing the part in CAD and having it in hand about an hour later.
claims.quote_verbatim: you draw it up in the cab, you send it to the machine. And an hour later you have your part
claims.speaker: Julia Truchsess

claims.claim_text: At least one printer vendor built a closed system that withheld user control of temperature and other print parameters in order to force purchases of its own material; the system was reverse engineered and an aftermarket temperature controller sold for it.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's a closed system where they tried to encourage people to buy only their materials by, uh, not allowing the user to control the temperature and other parameters of the printing process
claims.speaker: Julia Truchsess

claims.claim_text: Before affordable printing existed, prototype enclosures were hand-made from fiberglass and hand spray-painted; they looked like finished cases but were fragile enough that a set could not be entrusted to a courier or a flight and had to be driven to the trade show.
claims.quote_verbatim: they were like delicate handmade fiberglass cases
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A first print typically fails on build-plate adhesion rather than on geometry: a simple part printed correctly but could not be separated from its raft, and printing without a raft only worked once the build-surface tape had been cleaned.
claims.quote_verbatim: it won't print without the raft on the bottom
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Build-surface preparation is the undocumented step that decides whether raftless printing succeeds, and the knowledge circulates through forums rather than through documentation.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's because you haven't cleaned your capped on tape before you started
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: First-layer adhesion is the recurring troubleshooting problem for new users, with a glue stick on the build surface as the standard remedy; the transferable skill is understanding slicer configuration generically rather than following instructions for one machine.
claims.quote_verbatim: how do you troubleshoot my first layers not sticking
claims.speaker: Shawn Hymel

claims.claim_text: Filament degrades in storage: three-year-old material broke repeatedly inside the printer until it was replaced.
claims.quote_verbatim: I was using three-year-old filament. I kept breaking in the printer.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Psst...Hey buddy, wanna buy an Octopus?

claims.claim_text: Resin prints require a cleaning step in isopropyl alcohol after printing, which makes the process dependent on a consumable that is not always available.
claims.quote_verbatim: you've got to clean them with isopropyl
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Once a machine is correctly set up it should not need further adjustment, so the skill worth acquiring is not the printing itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: Once it's dialed in, you should never have to touch it again
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The selection criterion that matters for a working machine is the size of its user community and depth of support rather than headline specifications, so that any problem encountered has already been solved and documented by someone else.
claims.quote_verbatim: I need most supported, most community
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Picking a Pick and Place Pickiness

claims.claim_text: Deliberately staying on well-supported, slightly older equipment means never running out of forum threads when a problem appears.
claims.quote_verbatim: every time I have a problem, I want someone else to already have figured it out
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Picking a Pick and Place Pickiness

claims.claim_text: A vendor that supplies filament tuned to its own machines removes a variable from the workflow, so that a user who stays on the supported path does not have to think about material parameters at all.
claims.quote_verbatim: Prusa makes their own filament too, but it's like super dialed in
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The capability that determines whether a printer is useful is 3D modelling rather than printing: without modelling skill, the machine only reproduces objects other people designed.
claims.quote_verbatim: the hobby starts as 3D printing, but if it doesn't immediately become 3D modeling, basically, it's like you're just printing trinkets
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Slicing software matured to the point where the operational skill could be acquired in a few hours, shifting the difficulty entirely onto the modelling side.
claims.quote_verbatim: I learned it in three hours, you know, like how to slice something up and print something
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Shifting Away From DIY - Pedetentious PnP Progress

claims.claim_text: Printers consume a solid model in STL form, so mechanical CAD output has to be converted, and conversion quality varies between tools.
claims.quote_verbatim: 3D printing wants the STL solid model file
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Design Reviews Are Important - Habitual Hype Hebetude

claims.claim_text: Keeping a board as real solid-body geometry — a positive extrusion for the copper along the Z axis and a negative for the solder mask — is what makes downstream conversion reliable, because thermal finite-element analysis, milling CAM and printing each mesh the model differently and opportunistically.
claims.quote_verbatim: If I want to 3D print something, it's much easier to start with a solid body

claims.claim_text: Printing the board itself is used as a physical check on the electromechanical design: a test fit for connectors, and confirmation that mounting holes are in the right place and that the screws intended for them actually pass through.
claims.quote_verbatim: so that I can do things like a test fit for connectors or make sure that the holes are in the right location

claims.claim_text: An early electromechanical workflow was to export the board's 3D view into a free mechanical CAD package, design the case around it there and export a printable file through a plugin, putting a complete prototype within reach of about a hundred dollars.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can use Google SketchUp as a CAD tool to design your case around that board
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Analog Devices, Design Spark - Unusual Usenet Usurpation

claims.claim_text: The board model is imported into the mechanical tool purely as a reference for the enclosure, since nothing further can be done to the board there.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't do anything extra in it in SketchUp
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Analog Devices, Design Spark - Unusual Usenet Usurpation

claims.claim_text: A design detail that exploits the material: a six millimetre hole in polylactic acid takes a quarter-inch camera-mount screw driven directly into the plastic, the coarse threads gripping without an insert, which opens up a large ecosystem of tripod and clamp hardware.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you make a six millimeter hole, you can just take a quarter 20
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Captive nuts should be designed as a slot open at the top so that the nut drops in as the part prints; pausing the print to insert a nut horizontally and printing over it does not work.
claims.quote_verbatim: I actually like built up these supports, pause the print, inserted a nut, and then tried printing over top of it. And that is not the way to do it.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Wall thickness at a connector opening has to be sized from the mating cable's overmould rather than the connector alone: a thick-walled printed case blocked a USB-C cable whose overmould is specified at roughly six and a half by thirteen and a half millimetres maximum, requiring a recess.
claims.quote_verbatim: that overmold is spec'd as, like, 6.5 by 13.5
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: An early stereolithography print collapsed under its own geometry, a reminder that a shape that slices successfully is not necessarily one the process can hold.
claims.quote_verbatim: the first ever 3D print I did that was SLA-based, and it, like, caved in on itself
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Printing onto fabric is done by printing a base layer, pausing to lay the fabric down and letting the heat of the next layer fuse the fabric between layers, embedding a rigid insert directly into textile.
claims.quote_verbatim: the heat from the next layer melts the fabric between the layers
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A proposed route to printed electronics was to deposit a conductive layer within a powder-sintering process so that vias could be built up from the bottom layer to the top.
claims.quote_verbatim: you could build up the vias from the bottom to the top side
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - The Ternary Tussle

claims.claim_text: The same idea extends to printing pockets for surface-mount components, halting the process midway to drop parts in and then continuing to build over them.
claims.quote_verbatim: You could even have pockets for surface mount components. You could stop the process halfway through and drop them in and then keep building up.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - The Ternary Tussle

claims.claim_text: The obstacle to embedding components during printing is thermal: the printed polymer would have to survive soldering temperatures, or the board disintegrates when the joints are made.
claims.quote_verbatim: Otherwise, yeah, you solder them and your board falls apart.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - The Ternary Tussle

claims.claim_text: A printed circuit-board process is not a substitute for a fabricated board; the industry it addresses is large companies that need to keep design work in house for intellectual-property reasons.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's not a replacement for a PCB
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A related route to a three-dimensional object without a printer is to laser-cut each layer from thin sheet material and stack the layers.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can actually cut out all of your layers, and then you can stick the layers one on top of the other
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Texas Instruments, OPA & Chevy Volt - Nerdy Neuroelectronic Neurosis

claims.claim_text: Products that are custom by definition, such as orthopaedic insoles, are the natural application, because every item differs and there is no volume to amortise a tool against.
claims.quote_verbatim: each item is custom by definition. So, that's what 3D printing is great at
claims.speaker: Ariel Briner
claims.episode_title: An interview with Ariel Briner of Cartesian Co

claims.claim_text: A general-purpose fabrication machine presents users with a blank-canvas problem: told that a machine will make anything, most people cannot say what they want made.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's like this blank canvas problem. People don't know what to make yet
claims.speaker: Ariel Briner
claims.episode_title: An interview with Ariel Briner of Cartesian Co

claims.claim_text: The clearest justification for a printed part is one nobody would ever tool for: printed holders for pogo-pin test fixtures are a case where the need, rather than the schedule, is what makes printing the right process.
claims.quote_verbatim: no one's going to injection mold that kind of thing
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: The Art Of Staying Interested In Electronics - Exponible Electronics Ennui

claims.claim_text: A printed jig matched to the board outline holds a small board flat and square during hand assembly and rework.
claims.quote_verbatim: just like a match the board outline and 3D printed
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Printed pick-and-place feeders are used to escape the roughly thousand-dollar cost of commercial feeders, on the understanding that they will not match commercial pedigree.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm sick and tired of paying a thousand dollars for a feeder when I can just 3d print one
claims.speaker: Chris Denney

claims.claim_text: One assembly-machine vendor publishes its strip feeder files so that owners print their own rather than buying them, selling the printed parts only as a convenience.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can print a lot of strip feeders, uh, yourself to all the, the files are online
claims.speaker: Stephen Hawes
claims.episode_title: A Benchtop Pick and Place with Stephen Hawes

claims.claim_text: Printed feeders on a prototype machine are a prototype-only solution: a machine shipped in volume with printed feeders will need moulded tooling for them.
claims.quote_verbatim: if they've 3D printed their feeders and things like that, well, that's not going to work, uh, you know, long term
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Printed parts are visually identifiable in product photographs, so extrusion layer lines in a vendor's images reveal that the unit shown is a prototype rather than a production build.
claims.quote_verbatim: They do look 3D printed. Definitely FDM.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Picking a Pick and Place Pickiness

claims.claim_text: Printed compliant mechanisms are a distinctive capability: an open-source microscope is printed as a single fourteen-hour part with flexures built into it, using lever-action gearing to scale a motor's motion down to tens of microns.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's a big, crazy, like 14 hour 3d print that has a bunch of flexures baked into it
claims.speaker: Stephen Hawes
claims.episode_title: A Benchtop Pick and Place with Stephen Hawes

claims.claim_text: A printed mechanism that must operate repeatedly needs cycle testing rather than a single successful demonstration: a printer tool changer facing three hundred changes in a single multi-material part was cycle tested overnight, with a camera used to capture where it broke around the two hundred and fiftieth cycle.
claims.quote_verbatim: that could be like 300 tool changes and it needs to work perfectly every single time
claims.episode_title: Grad School Time Capsule with Joshua and Zach

claims.claim_text: Filming a repeated test is what makes an intermittent mechanical failure diagnosable, since the failure is otherwise discovered only after the fact.
claims.quote_verbatim: I had to set up a bunch of like cycle testing
claims.episode_title: Grad School Time Capsule with Joshua and Zach

claims.claim_text: Printed parts serve as the pattern for metal casting: a printed pattern used with lost-pattern sand casting produced an intake manifold, a curved and complex shape that would be impractical to machine and undesirable to split into a two-part assembly.
claims.quote_verbatim: casting, I think, is uniquely suited to making intake manifolds
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: The limit on printed casting patterns is build volume: large patterns have to be made in multiple pieces, which leaves a seam in the finished metal part.
claims.quote_verbatim: the parts tend to be big. So you need to make them out of multiple pieces
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: Printing is the iteration mechanism in an electrical and mechanical co-design workflow carried out by a single engineer with a single toolchain.
claims.quote_verbatim: using 3D printing to sort of be doing iterative development
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: Printing a set of construction-toy-compatible beams — eight millimetres wide with holes eight millimetres centre to centre — gives a mechanical sketching medium that removes the blank-page problem at the start of a design, with the properly designed part following afterwards.
claims.quote_verbatim: eight millimeters wide and the holes are eight millimeters center to center
claims.speaker: Jason Huggins

claims.claim_text: Having a physical bucket of standard parts on the desk to build with is a deliberate first step in mechanical design, with the from-scratch design done after the arrangement is understood.
claims.quote_verbatim: I need a bucket, I need it like a box or a bucket of parts on my desk and I just start building
claims.speaker: Jason Huggins

claims.claim_text: Keeping a design printable makes it reproducible locally from published files, which avoids international shipping and the customs costs that make exporting finished hardware to some countries impractical.
claims.quote_verbatim: part of the reason why I wanted to keep my designs as 3d printable as possible is so people could download the plans and make it locally
claims.speaker: Jason Huggins

claims.claim_text: Where machining is not accessible, designers deliberately restrict themselves to printable geometry, and a printed capstan drive or gear reduction can be produced at a fraction of the cost of a machined metal gearbox with high precision.
claims.quote_verbatim: I won't really design something to be machined unless I 100% need it to be machined
claims.speaker: Aaed Musa

claims.claim_text: Custom printed drivetrain components can be cheaper than buying a metal planetary gearbox while remaining precise enough for the application.
claims.quote_verbatim: could just 3d print one that, you know, is a fraction of the cost
claims.speaker: Aaed Musa

claims.claim_text: A humanoid robot programme moved from vacuum-formed shells to fully printed structural parts, with aluminium extrusion and steel brackets carrying load internally, and simulated the joints in CAD before printing.
claims.quote_verbatim: all of it was 3D printed instead of doing like vacuum forming
claims.speaker: James Bruton

claims.claim_text: Printing lowers the cost of mechanical prototyping enough that trial and error becomes the working method for someone without formal mechanical training.
claims.quote_verbatim: 3D printing allows you to prototype stuff pretty cheaply
claims.speaker: James Bruton

claims.claim_text: Custom mechanism development is where printing earned its place in one machine-building practice, alongside existing CNC and laser capability, and throughput was raised by running several machines in parallel rather than by buying a faster one.
claims.quote_verbatim: I need more 3d printer bandwidth
claims.speaker: Ben Heck

claims.claim_text: Print speed is fast enough to fit inside a one-week concept-to-finished-project cycle, which is why projects on that schedule are designed around printing rather than around machining.
claims.quote_verbatim: 3d printing is fast enough that I can actually do it on the one week schedule
claims.speaker: Zack Freedman

claims.claim_text: Individual prints still take hours, so a print has to be started and collected around other work rather than watched.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's a 3D print. It takes six hours
claims.speaker: Zack Freedman

claims.claim_text: Prints rarely finish in under an hour or two, which makes utilisation and cost amortisation difficult for shared-access workshops charging per use.
claims.quote_verbatim: There's hardly ever a print I've done that takes less than an hour or two.

claims.claim_text: A printed model answers ergonomic and fit questions that cannot be settled from a drawing: printing a device mock-up so that people could carry it in a pocket established whether the electronics would fit the intended form factor.
claims.quote_verbatim: why don't we just 3d print a model of the device? And then you can have people put it in their pockets and see how well it fits
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A printed case prototype in clear resin communicates the look and feel of a product in a way images cannot, which is why manufacturers send them before tooling.
claims.quote_verbatim: they sent me this clear resin printed prototype thing
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The iteration rate available in mechanical prototyping — three complete sets of prints inside two days — has no equivalent in electronics, where parts alone may not arrive in that time.
claims.quote_verbatim: he'll have three sets of prints in, you know, two days
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A rough print that is only good enough to reveal that a model is the wrong size is a legitimate use of the process, since the check costs a few hours and no tooling.
claims.quote_verbatim: to be able to even throw a rough model into my printer and then be like, oh, that was way too small
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Printing a scale replica of a mechanism described in a paper is a way of understanding how it works, as was done with a nanometre-accuracy micro-positioning stage.
claims.quote_verbatim: he 3D printed a replica, like a miniature scale replica
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A proof of concept assembled from an off-the-shelf development board, a custom sensor board on its standard pinout and a printed case cost perhaps ten to twenty times the eventual unit cost but was delivered on the schedule the client needed.
claims.quote_verbatim: it was probably, I don't know, 10, 20 times what it would cost in a final
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The economics of one-off and small-batch work have inverted: material cost used to rival the non-recurring engineering cost at quantities of one or ten, whereas material is now cheap and engineering time remains expensive.
claims.quote_verbatim: the cost of material is, is so cheap and NREs is still expensive
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Tooling cost has effectively disappeared for low-run prototypes, so a one-person operation can produce hundreds of well-finished units without amortising a tool.
claims.quote_verbatim: There's basically no tooling cost anymore.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Service bureaus give access to machines an individual could not justify: a five-hundred-dollar desktop machine owner can send a job to a hundred-thousand-dollar machine and pay only for material and time.
claims.quote_verbatim: I've got a $500 kit printer, but I can go and print something on their $100,000 printer and just pay for the material and time
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Distributed printing marketplaces differ from bureaus in owning no machines: they locate the nearest privately owned printer, list its capabilities and price, and act purely as a transaction layer.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's literally just a transaction layer
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The same routing to a nearby owner-operated machine is what makes local printing available without a bureau's central factory.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can see who the closest 3D printer is to you and then you can, they list the price
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: The Art Of Staying Interested In Electronics - Exponible Electronics Ennui

claims.claim_text: The buy-versus-outsource arithmetic favours outsourcing for most users: a good desktop machine at about two thousand dollars buys roughly forty bureau prints at around fifty dollars each, more than most people order in a year unless they are iterating heavily.
claims.quote_verbatim: So that's what, 40 prints.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Bureau pricing carries a large premium over material cost: a tennis-ball-sized part cost about a hundred and fifty dollars rush-printed at a commercial bureau against roughly twenty dollars at a shared workspace charging material only, but the shared machine ran just once a week.
claims.quote_verbatim: shapeways charged me about $150 for that
claims.speaker: Greg Davill

claims.claim_text: The trade between the cheap shared machine and the expensive bureau is a schedule one, since the shared machine's weekly run sets the earliest possible delivery.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's only the only run it once a week.
claims.speaker: Greg Davill

claims.claim_text: Low-cost board fabricators added printing services at prices low enough to weaken the case for owning a machine at all.
claims.quote_verbatim: all of the PCB houses are doing it too
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Most people working in this space do not need to own the equipment: the work can be sent out, and a great deal can still be accomplished with a Dremel and a file.
claims.quote_verbatim: most people do not need a lot of this equipment
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Printing is a standard step in the product development process for consumer products generally, which is distinct from its role as a consumer manufacturing method in the home.
claims.quote_verbatim: I would challenge you to find a single consumer product that's designed today that doesn't make heavy use of 3D printing in the product development process
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: The technology's real effect is argued to resemble precision casting rather than the semiconductor: a genuinely important process whose consequences reach consumers only indirectly, and which does not threaten commodity injection moulding of items costing fractions of a penny.
claims.quote_verbatim: that thing costs fractions of a penny to make

claims.claim_text: Printed metal parts are difficult to edit once designed, which is why topology optimisation software exists and why the design method for them differs fundamentally from conventional modelling.
claims.quote_verbatim: even if you do design it, then they're really hard to edit

claims.claim_text: Full-colour printing only pays off if the part was designed for it and the colour routed through the geometry, rather than an existing model being sent to a colour machine.
claims.quote_verbatim: unless you're thinking about this when you're actually designing the part
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: A Jumperless Breadboard with Kevin Cappuccio

claims.claim_text: Four-dimensional printing refers to printing an object that changes shape after fabrication, unfolding into its final form when placed in water.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's the one where it prints and then you like stick it in water and it like unfolds and it makes a different shape.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Low-cost machines from Chinese manufacturers arrived calibrated well enough to print acceptably after roughly ten minutes of setup, removing the assembly-and-tuning stage that earlier kits required.
claims.quote_verbatim: it set up in 10 minutes

claims.claim_text: The prototype watch shown for a widely funded wearable campaign was one of three stereolithography prints, including a transparent printed lens that was painstakingly polished afterwards and cost about a thousand dollars each for the lens alone.
claims.quote_verbatim: they were 3d printed including the lens
claims.speaker: Andrew Witte
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Andrew Witte - Telistic Timepiece Technomania

claims.claim_text: Printed plastics were not strong enough to serve as a working case, so the display was crammed into the printed shell, the remaining volume filled with RTV to stiffen it, and the electronics tethered outside on a separate prototype board.
claims.quote_verbatim: the 3d printed plastics are not very strong
claims.speaker: Andrew Witte
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Andrew Witte - Telistic Timepiece Technomania

claims.claim_text: Filling the void in a printed shell with a curing compound is a practical way to make a fragile printed prototype solid enough to handle.
claims.quote_verbatim: filled the rest of it with i don't know rtv or something to make it more solid
claims.speaker: Andrew Witte
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Andrew Witte - Telistic Timepiece Technomania

claims.claim_text: Electronics engineers increasingly carry responsibility for packaging as well as circuits, and printing is what makes prototype packaging feasible for them without a mechanical department.
claims.quote_verbatim: I've been doing 3D printing at work just because I'm expected to do packaging and electronics now
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
